nameStory: The Yellow-shouldered Slug Moth gets its name from the bright yellow patches on its forewings that look like little shoulder pads. The "slug" part refers to its caterpillar stage, which crawls around looking remarkably like a tiny, colorful slug with no visible legs. It's also called the ochre-winged hag moth, with "hag" being an old term for moths that were considered magical or mysterious.
description: The Yellow-shouldered Slug Moth is a small, chunky moth with distinctive yellow shoulder patches on brown wings. As adults, they're compact moths that hold their wings tent-like over their bodies when at rest. Their caterpillars are the real showstoppers - smooth, slug-like creatures that glide along leaves without any visible legs. The whole family is called "slug moths" because of these unusual caterpillars that look nothing like typical fuzzy moth larvae.

idTips.label: Compact body shape
idTips.description: Small, stocky moth that sits with wings held in a tent-like position over a robust, hairy body

idTips.label: Brown wing coloration
idTips.description: Rich brown or chocolate-colored wings with the yellow patches creating a striking contrast

idTips.label: Slug-like caterpillar
idTips.description: If you find the larva, it's smooth and jelly-like with no visible legs, gliding along leaf surfaces like a tiny green or yellow slug

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Small moth with wings spanning roughly an inch across when fully spread

habitat: Look for Yellow-shouldered Slug Moths in deciduous woodlands and forest edges throughout New England, especially where oak, cherry, and maple trees grow. The adults are attracted to lights at night, so you might spot them around porch lights or at moth sheets near wooded areas. Their caterpillars feed on the leaves of various hardwood trees, so they're most common in mixed forests rather than pure coniferous stands.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring, usually May into early June. Look for them at lights during warm evenings.
seasonality.summer: Peak flight time is early to mid-summer when adults are most active. Caterpillars can be found on tree leaves, looking like tiny slugs.
seasonality.fall: Late-season adults may still be flying in early fall, while caterpillars prepare for winter by dropping to the ground to pupate.
seasonality.winter: Overwintering as pupae in the soil or leaf litter. No above-ground activity during cold months.

funFact: The caterpillars of slug moths can actually sting you! Despite looking harmless and squishy, many species in this family have hidden venomous spines that can cause a painful burning sensation if you touch them - nature's way of making a slow-moving, soft caterpillar into a tiny tank that predators learn to avoid.
confusionNotes: The yellow shoulder patches make this species fairly distinctive among New England moths. However, worn or faded specimens might be confused with other small brown moths, but the bright yellow "shoulders" are usually still visible even in older individuals. Remember: yellow patches on the front of brown wings equals yellow-shouldered slug moth.
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the name "slug moth" fool you into thinking these are related to garden slugs - they're true moths whose caterpillars just happen to look and move like slugs. This is a perfect example of convergent evolution, where unrelated animals develop similar appearances to solve the same problems.
compareHints: As the only Lithacodes species regularly found in New England, the Yellow-shouldered Slug Moth is distinctive within its genus. Compared to other slug moths in the region, it's the only one with those bright yellow shoulder patches on brown wings. Other slug moths might be green, have different patterns, or lack the distinctive yellow coloration that makes this species so recognizable.
